body:
Background of the Salt Satyagraha

At its Lahore session in December 1929, the Indian National Congress adopted the objective of Purna Swaraj, or complete independence. Gandhi subsequently selected the British salt law as the subject of a major non-violent campaign.

The colonial government controlled the manufacture and sale of salt and imposed a tax on it. Since salt was an essential commodity consumed by people irrespective of their economic or social position, opposition to the salt law could unite different sections of society.

Gandhi therefore decided to demonstrate resistance to colonial authority by producing or collecting salt in violation of the law.

Beginning of the Dandi March

On 12 March 1930, Mahatma Gandhi departed from Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad with 78 selected companions. The original marching group therefore consisted of Gandhi and 78 other participants.

The march covered approximately 390 km, conventionally described as 241 miles, and is generally remembered as a 24-day march. During the journey, Gandhi addressed people in villages and towns and explained the objectives of the movement.

Geographical course of the march

The route passed through central and southern Gujarat before reaching the Arabian Sea coast at Dandi in present-day Navsari district.

Important places along the route, in their historical sequence, included Sabarmati Ashram, Aslali, Bareja, Nadiad, Anand, Borsad, Ras, Jambusar, Bharuch, Ankleshwar, Surat, Navsari, Matwad and Dandi. These were selected places along a longer route containing numerous intermediate stops.

Arrival and breaking of the salt law

Gandhi reached Dandi on 5 April 1930. On the following day, 6 April 1930, he broke the British salt law by collecting natural salt from the seashore.

This symbolic act demonstrated that an unjust colonial law could be challenged through peaceful and deliberate disobedience. It marked the beginning of widespread civil disobedience against British rule.

3 important dates

  • 12 March 1930: Departure from Sabarmati Ashram.
  • 5 April 1930: Arrival at Dandi.
  • 6 April 1930: Breaking of the salt law at Dandi.

Number of participants

Gandhi initially selected 78 companions for the march. Satish Kalelkar and Kharag Bahadur Singh joined the marching party on 14 March 1930, bringing the number of companions to 80.

This distinction explains why the historical departure is associated with 78 companions, while the National Salt Satyagraha Memorial at Dandi commemorates Gandhi and 80 marchers.

Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience

Non-cooperation primarily involved withdrawing support from colonial institutions and economic arrangements. Civil disobedience went further by deliberately violating particular unjust laws in a non-violent manner.

The act of collecting salt at Dandi was an example of civil disobedience because it directly challenged an existing law rather than merely withdrawing cooperation from the government.

Continuation of the Salt Satyagraha

The Salt Satyagraha continued after the events at Dandi. Gandhi was arrested at Karadi on 5 May 1930 before he could lead a proposed campaign at the Dharasana salt works.

Abbas Tyabji subsequently assumed leadership of the campaign. After his arrest, Sarojini Naidu took a leading role in the Dharasana Satyagraha.

Thus, Dandi and Dharasana were associated with the same wider movement but represented separate historical episodes.

Prelims focus

  • Starting point: Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad.
  • Destination: Dandi, present-day Navsari district.
  • Departure: 12 March 1930, with 78 companions.
  • Distance: Approximately 390 km or 241 miles.
  • The salt law was broken on 6 April 1930.
  • Trap: Arrival at Dandi on 5 April and breaking the salt law on 6 April were separate events.

[References: NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts-III, 2020–2021 reprint, Chapter 9, The March to Dandi, pp. 121–122; NCERT, Class 10, India and the Contemporary World-II, Nationalism in India, pp. 63–64; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part III, The Salt Satyagraha: A Case Study, pp. 355–359; GCERT, Class 8 Social Science, Gujarati-medium edition, Chapter 6, Dandi March; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Chronology of the Dandi March and Post-Dandi March Events; Sabarmati Ashram Preservation and Memorial Trust, History. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Historical importance of Dandi

Dandi is a coastal village in Jalalpore taluka of Navsari district, Gujarat. Its national importance arises from the Salt Satyagraha of 6 April 1930, when Gandhi challenged the British monopoly over salt.

The village preserves historical places directly associated with Gandhi's arrival and protest, as well as modern memorial structures constructed to commemorate the event.

Saifee Villa

Saifee Villa is a historical building associated with Gandhi's stay at Dandi. Gandhi stayed there on the night of 5 April 1930 before breaking the salt law on the following day.

The building houses a museum and library associated with Gandhi and the Salt Satyagraha. Its importance rests on its direct historical association with the events of April 1930.

Other commemorative landmarks at Dandi include Prarthna Mandir, associated with Gandhi's prayer and public address, and Kirti Stambh, which commemorates the Salt Satyagraha.

National Salt Satyagraha Memorial

The National Salt Satyagraha Memorial was dedicated to the nation on 30 January 2019, the death anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi.

The memorial was developed under the Ministry of Culture, Government of India, with the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay playing an important role in its design coordination and implementation.

The memorial communicates the history of the Salt March through sculptures, narrative murals, commemorative structures and educational activities.

Important features of the memorial

  • Statue of Mahatma Gandhi: A 5-metre-high statue commemorating his leadership of the Salt March.
  • 80 bronze statues: Represent the marchers who accompanied Gandhi.
  • 24 narrative murals: Depict events and themes associated with the historic march.
  • Artificial lake: Represents the coastal setting of the Salt Satyagraha.
  • Salt-making pans: Provide visitors with an educational experience of salt production.
  • 41 solar trees: Designed to meet the memorial's energy requirements through solar power, reflecting the principle of self-sufficiency.

The combination of sculptures and narrative reliefs transforms the memorial into a place of historical education. Visitors can understand both the collective nature of the march and the significance of salt as a symbol of resistance.

Historical participant count and memorial representation

The 80 statues of marchers must not be confused with the 78 companions who originally departed from Sabarmati Ashram. Satish Kalelkar and Kharag Bahadur Singh joined during the journey.

Historical site and modern memorial

Saifee Villa is important because Gandhi stayed there during the actual historical event in 1930. The National Salt Satyagraha Memorial is a later commemorative institution dedicated in 2019. Both preserve the same historical legacy, but they belong to different periods.

Prelims focus

  • Dandi is situated in Jalalpore taluka, Navsari district.
  • Saifee Villa is associated with Gandhi's stay on 5 April 1930.
  • The National Salt Satyagraha Memorial was dedicated on 30 January 2019.
  • The memorial contains 80 statues of marchers and 24 narrative murals.
  • IIT Bombay participated in the memorial's development.
  • Trap: The 80 commemorated marchers and the original 78 companions are not contradictory figures.

[References: District Navsari, Government of Gujarat, Dandi; National Salt Satyagraha Memorial, About, Attractions and Project Information; Press Information Bureau, Dedication of the National Salt Satyagraha Memorial, 30 January 2019; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Chronology of the Dandi March. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Birthplace of Mahatma Gandhi

Porbandar is a coastal city in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat. Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born there on 2 October 1869.

His father, Karamchand Gandhi, also known as Kaba Gandhi, served as Diwan of Porbandar. His mother was Putlibai.

The ancestral house in which Gandhi was born is preserved as part of the Kirti Mandir heritage complex. The actual room of his birth is situated within this historical residential building.

Establishment of Kirti Mandir

Kirti Mandir was developed as a memorial to Mahatma Gandhi and Kasturba Gandhi adjoining the original ancestral house.

Industrialist and philanthropist Nanjibhai Kalidas Mehta acquired the ancestral property with Gandhi's consent and supported the construction of the memorial.

The foundation stone was laid in 1947 by Darbar Gopaldas Desai. The memorial was designed and constructed by architect Purushottambhai Mistry.

Kirti Mandir was dedicated to the nation on 27 May 1950 by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

Architectural symbolism

The memorial is approximately 79 feet high, symbolising Gandhi's life, which ended during his 79th year. Gandhi died on 30 January 1948 at the age of 78 completed years.

Kirti Mandir incorporates architectural motifs associated with 6 religious traditions:

  • Hinduism
  • Jainism
  • Buddhism
  • Islam
  • Christianity
  • Zoroastrianism

These elements express Gandhi's belief in respect for different religious traditions. The name Kirti Mandir refers to its memorial character; it is not a shrine devoted exclusively to the worship of a particular deity.

Museum and educational significance

The Kirti Mandir complex contains historical photographs, memorial displays, a library and material associated with Gandhi's life. The preservation of his ancestral house allows visitors to understand the domestic setting of his early life.

The birthplace and the memorial must be distinguished chronologically. The original house existed when Gandhi was born in 1869, whereas Kirti Mandir is the adjoining memorial dedicated in 1950.

Prelims focus

  • Gandhi was born at Porbandar on 2 October 1869.
  • Kirti Mandir commemorates Mahatma Gandhi and Kasturba Gandhi.
  • Principal patron: Nanjibhai Kalidas Mehta.
  • Architect: Purushottambhai Mistry.
  • Dedicated by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel on 27 May 1950.
  • The memorial is approximately 79 feet high.

[References: District Porbandar, Government of Gujarat, Kirti Mandir; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Kirti Mandir, Porbandar, historical background and present structure; Kirti Mandir Management Committee, history and architectural information. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Heritage routes and historical memory

A heritage route connects places associated with a common historical event, cultural tradition or movement. Its significance arises not only from individual buildings and monuments but also from the historical relationship between the places along the route.

The Sabarmati–Dandi route is an important example of a heritage route connected with India's freedom struggle. It commemorates the journey undertaken by Mahatma Gandhi and his companions during the Salt Satyagraha of 1930.

The preservation of places along this route helps explain how a political movement originating at an ashram in Ahmedabad developed into a mass campaign extending across Gujarat and other parts of India.

Commemoration of Gandhian heritage

Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav

On 12 March 2021, a commemorative Dandi Padyatra was launched from Sabarmati Ashram as part of the inauguration of Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav, the national programme commemorating 75 years of India's independence.

The selection of 12 March and Sabarmati Ashram recalled the original departure of Gandhi for Dandi on 12 March 1930.

Restoration of Gandhian sites

On 12 March 2024, the restored Kochrab Ashram was inaugurated. On the same occasion, the master plan for the Gandhi Ashram Memorial redevelopment at Sabarmati was launched.

The inauguration of a restored historical building must be distinguished from its original establishment. Kochrab Ashram dates to 1915, while the 2024 event concerned its restoration. The launch of the Sabarmati redevelopment master plan was a project milestone, not a declaration that all redevelopment work had been completed.

UNESCO Tentative List

A UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List is an inventory of properties that a country considers suitable for possible future nomination to the World Heritage List. Inclusion in the Tentative List does not itself confer World Heritage Site status.

The 2014 Satyagraha heritage proposal

On 15 April 2014, India submitted a cultural heritage proposal concerning sites associated with its non-violent freedom movement.

Among the Gujarat components identified in this proposal were Kochrab Ashram, Sabarmati Ashram and the Dandi March route. The proposal was submitted under cultural criteria (iv) and (vi).

The 2026 transnational Satyagraha proposal

On 3 September 2026, India submitted another cultural heritage proposal titled The Sites of Satyagraha: The Emergence and institutionalization of the non-violent movement.

The proposal is transnational, involving India and South Africa, and includes 9 component sites: 7 in India and 2 in South Africa. It was submitted under cultural criteria (iii) and (vi).

Sabarmati Ashram is the only Gujarat component of the 2026 proposal. Kochrab Ashram, Dandi and Kirti Mandir at Porbandar are not listed as components of this particular proposal.

Feature2014 proposal2026 proposal
Submission date15 April 20143 September 2026
Participating countriesIndiaIndia and South Africa
Cultural criteria(iv), (vi)(iii), (vi)
Principal Gujarat sites relevant hereKochrab, Sabarmati, Dandi routeSabarmati
Status on 26 November 2026Tentative ListTentative List

Tentative listing is not inscription

As of 26 November 2026, both Satyagraha proposals remain on India's UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List. They must not be described as inscribed World Heritage Sites.

Importance of preserving Gandhian heritage

Gandhian heritage includes physical evidence, such as historical residences, ashram buildings, spinning wheels, photographs and original correspondence, as well as the continuing transmission of Gandhian principles and practices.

Museums preserve and interpret objects and documents. Historical buildings retain the original setting of important events. Heritage routes connect geographically separated places associated with a common movement. Educational visits and exhibitions help communicate the significance of all these forms of heritage.

Integrated revision of the principal sites

The 4 principal locations represent different stages of Gandhi's life and legacy. Porbandar represents his birth and the memorial dedicated in 1950. Kochrab represents the establishment of his first Indian ashram in 1915. Sabarmati represents the development of his social and political work from 1917 to 1930, together with the Gandhi Memorial Museum inaugurated in 1963. Dandi represents the breaking of the salt law on 6 April 1930 and the National Salt Satyagraha Memorial dedicated in 2019.

Prelims focus

  • The historical Dandi March route connects Sabarmati Ashram with Dandi.
  • The commemorative Dandi Padyatra of 2021 was associated with Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav.
  • The restored Kochrab Ashram was inaugurated on 12 March 2024.
  • The 2014 UNESCO tentative proposal includes Kochrab, Sabarmati and the Dandi March route.
  • The 2026 transnational proposal involves India and South Africa; Sabarmati is its only Gujarat component.
  • Trap: UNESCO Tentative List inclusion does not amount to World Heritage inscription.

[References: GCERT, Class 10 Social Science, Gujarati-medium edition, Chapter 7, Preservation of Our Heritage, pp. 59–60; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Culture Year End Review 2021, 31 December 2021; Press Information Bureau, Inauguration of Kochrab Ashram and Launch of the Gandhi Ashram Memorial Master Plan, 12 March 2024; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Sites of Saytagrah, India's non-violent freedom movement, Tentative List reference 5899, submitted 15 April 2014; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, The Sites of Satyagraha: The Emergence and institutionalization of the non-violent movement, Tentative List reference 7042, submitted 3 September 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, India's Tentative List. Online sources and listing status consulted 26 November 2026.]
